name: Simulation output
text:
# Simulation output


## Overview
This family covers methods that generate volumetric data by simulating physical phenomena (fluids, fire, smoke) or kinematic systems, producing a discrete or analytic representation suitable for rendering. Unlike [Voxelization](12-voxelization.md) which converts static geometry, or [Procedural and implicit volumes](13-procedural-and-implicit-volumes.md) which define volume via analytic functions, simulation output methods evolve state over time based on physical laws (e.g., Navier-Stokes, Position-Based Dynamics) or kinematic rules. The core mechanism involves defining a spatial domain (grid or particles), evolving physical quantities (velocity, density, temperature) through time-stepping, and storing the result in a structure (voxel grid, particle list, or Gaussian kernel) that serves as the input for a volume renderer.

## Shared principles
All methods in this family map a conceptual or physical source into a discrete or analytic volumetric representation suitable for rendering [G]. The core mechanism involves:
1. **Domain Definition**: Establishing a spatial domain, typically a 3D grid with resolution $(N_x, N_y, N_z)$ and bounding box, or an infinite analytic space [G].
2. **Value Assignment**: Determining the value (density, distance, color) for each point in the domain based on the source method (geometric intersection, function evaluation, or physical state) [G].
3. **Storage/Access**: Either storing the result in a discrete array ([voxelization](#12-voxelization.md), simulation) or providing an interface to compute it on-the-fly (procedural) [G].

## Subtopics

### [Gaussian Splashing](1387-gaussian-splashing.md)
[Gaussian Splashing](#1387-gaussian-splashing.md) (GSP) combines 3D [Gaussian Splatting](#946-gaussian-splatting.md) with Position-Based Dynamics (PBD) to simulate fluids, deformable bodies, and rigid objects. It solves the limitation of vanilla 3DGS, which lacks well-defined appearance properties for translucent/specular fluids, by enriching Gaussian kernels with material parameters (diffusiveness, specularity, roughness) and aligning kernel orientation with surface normals. Choose this when interactive, [physically-based rendering](#6815-physically-based-rendering-pbr-lighting.md) of deformable objects from novel views is required.

### [Position Based Fluids](1765-position-based-fluids.md)
[Position Based Fluids](#1765-position-based-fluids.md) (PBF) is a Lagrangian particle-based method that enforces incompressibility by iteratively correcting particle positions based on density constraints. It distinguishes itself from Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) by treating fluid dynamics as a constraint satisfaction problem rather than solving Navier-Stokes equations via pressure gradients, offering superior stability for incompressible flows. Choose this for real-time, [stable fluid](#7906-stable-fluids-gpu-implementation.md) simulation where meshing is undesirable.

### [Voxel-based 3D Fire Simulation](3411-voxel-based-3d-fire-simulation.md)
This method simulates fire dynamics by storing velocity, smoke density, temperature, and fuel level in a discrete 3D voxel grid. It solves the Navier-Stokes equations augmented by buoyancy and vorticity forces to model rising, curling fire. It is distinguished from particle-based methods by its structured grid storage, allowing efficient divergence and advection calculations using 3D textures. Choose this for [grid-based fire](#3411-voxel-based-3d-fire-simulation.md) and smoke effects with explicit physical coupling.

### [Smoke Advection](4639-smoke-advection.md)
[Smoke advection](#4639-smoke-advection.md) tracks scalar quantities (density, temperature, color) transported by a fluid velocity field to visualize smoke or fire. It solves the advection equation using the MacCormack method. Unlike velocity, these quantities are primarily visual, though temperature can influence dynamics via buoyancy. Choose this for visualizing passive or coupled scalars in an existing velocity field.

### [GPU-based Fluid Simulation with Voxel Rendering](7400-gpu-based-fluid-simulation-with-voxel-rendering.md)
This method integrates real-time incompressible fluid simulation with [sparse voxel-based rasterization](#2464-svraster.md) on graphics hardware, using Direct3D geometry [shaders for rendering](#1495-in-shader-neural-volume-ray-marching.md) and compute shaders for simulation. It solves the problem of efficiently visualizing dynamic fluid volumes by bypassing CPU-GPU data transfer bottlenecks. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on CPU-side voxel activation, this approach moves voxel activation and color ramping directly into the [geometry shader](#4369-geometry-shader-quads.md), using stream-out to guarantee deterministic ordering. Choose this for high-performance, GPU-native voxel rendering of fluids.

### [Niagara Fluids Volume Rendering](7739-niagara-fluids-volume-rendering.md)
[Niagara Fluids Volume Rendering](#7739-niagara-fluids-volume-rendering.md) repurposes Unreal Engine’s grid-based fluid simulation system for volume rendering by ignoring the simulation step and utilizing only the rendering pipeline. It differs from dedicated volume renderers by leveraging the engine’s native Niagara particle system and material domain, allowing for interactive transfer function authoring within the Editor. Unlike [Gaussian Splashing](1387-gaussian-splashing.md) or [Position Based Fluids](1765-position-based-fluids.md), which generate geometry or particles, this method treats the simulation grid as a static volumetric texture container, albeit with significant memory overhead. Choose this for Unreal Engine environments requiring quick volume visualization without custom rendering code.

#### Smoke Source Injection
A Unity MonoBehaviour component that injects density and velocity into the Navier-Stokes solver at the transform's world position during `FixedUpdate` [S1, unofficial]. It uses parameters `smoke_amount` (float) for density addition, `smoke_initial_velocity` (Vector3) for velocity addition, and an unused `active` flag [S1, unofficial].

#### Fire Reaction Coordinate
A method tracking a reaction coordinate to simulate fire, indicating time since ignition and fuel exhaustion [S2, unofficial]. The coordinate $Y$ evolves as $\frac{\partial Y}{\partial t} = -(u \cdot \nabla)Y - k$, where $k$ is a constant decrement per time step [S2, unofficial]. A value of 1 indicates ignition, and $<0$ indicates exhaustion [S2, unofficial]. It is advected using `PS_ADVECT_MACCORMACK` with $k$ added to the result, and a spherical region is set to 1 to continuously generate fuel [S2, unofficial].

#### Buoyant Force for Smoke
Adds a buoyant force to the velocity field based on temperature differences to make hot smoke rise [S2, unofficial]. The force is calculated as $\mathbf{f}_{buoyancy} = \frac{Pmg}{R} \left( \frac{1}{T_0} - \frac{1}{T} \right) \mathbf{z}$, where $P$ is pressure, $m$ is molar mass, $g$ is gravity, $R$ is the gas constant, $T_0$ is ambient temperature, $T$ is advected temperature, and $\mathbf{z}$ is the upward vector [S2, unofficial]. This force is added to the velocity field immediately following velocity advection [S2, unofficial].

#### Massless Particle System
Particles are used as tracer elements to visualize flow, droplets for fire suppression, or fuel elements (embers) [S3, unofficial]. Positions are determined by $\frac{dx_p}{dt} = V(x_p, t)$, assuming drag force is large compared to gravity ($mg$) [S3, unofficial]. Particle size is specified via `glPointSize(partpointsize)` and streak line length in seconds [S3, unofficial]. Velocity field and particle motion are computed by FDS and communicated to Smokeview via data files [S3, unofficial].

#### Galaxy Kinematic Simulation
A kinematic approach to simulate galaxy time evolution using differential rotation laws and first-order integration, without full dynamic simulation [S4]. Gas and stars on the disk rotate according to a typical galaxy rotation curve, while bulge stars rotate with constant velocity balancing gravitational attraction [S4]. Equations of motion are integrated using first-order methods; numerical errors amplify, making the simulation meaningful for only a few hundred million years [S4]. Double precision is required for geometrical calculations to handle the large dynamic range [S4]. Used to render the galaxy component within cosmological simulations [S4].

## Background
Simulation-based [volume data generation](#11-producing-volume-data.md) has roots in computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and scientific visualization. Early methods focused on grid-based Eulerian approaches for smoke and fire, such as the [MacCormack advection scheme](#4952-maccormack-advection-scheme.md) described in GPU Gems [S2, unofficial]. Lagrangian methods like Position-Based Fluids emerged to address stability issues in particle-based simulations [S2, unofficial]. In scientific visualization, tools like Smokeview used massless particles and volumetric rendering to visualize Fire Dynamics Simulation (FDS) data [S3, unofficial]. More recently, kinematic simulations have been used in astrophysics to visualize galaxy evolution within cosmological contexts [S4]. The integration of these simulations with real-time rendering pipelines, such as GPU-based voxel rendering [S1, unofficial] and Gaussian Splatting [S3, unofficial], represents a shift towards interactive, physically-based visual effects.
